extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent attorneys, and law students studying patent specification drafting and claim construction
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules for drafting a patent specification and for courts/juries to construe patents — what must be described, how claims relate to the specification, and when a specification or patent is void for ambiguity or overbreadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and drawings form part of the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent is to be construed together with the specification (and drawings annexed) in order to ascertain the subject-matter of the invention; drawings annexed in compliance with the statute form part of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification may control the generality of the patent's terms. Drawings not accompanying the specification do not form part of it. (Cited cases: Whittemore v. Cutter; Washburn v. Gould; Brooks v. Bicknell.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court determines construction of patent; jury's role conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the province of the court to determine what is intended to be patented and whether the patent is valid as a question of law upon construction of the patent's terms; the jury takes the court's construction either absolutely or conditionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are no words of art or surrounding circumstances requiring factual inquiry, the jury must accept the court's construction absolutely. Where terms of art or surrounding circumstances affect meaning, the jury decides those facts and applies the court's conditional construction. (See Neilson v. Harford and related authorities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement assessed by factfinder with expert evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the invention is described with sufficient fullness, clearness, and exactness to enable a skilful person to put it in practice is a question for the jury (on evidence of experts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications are addressed to competent workmen familiar with the art; expert testimony is used to tell the jury whether the specification shows enough on its face to reproduce the invention without difficulty. (Authorities: Davis v. Palmer; Davoll v. Brown.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification may control generality of claims but cannot contradict letters patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification can limit or control the generality of the patent's terms, but if there is a clear repugnancy between the description in the specification and the invention stated in the letters patent, the patent is void because the statute is not complied with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule allowing specification to control the patent does not extend to cases of inconsistency between them. (Illustration: The King v. Wheeler where patent stated invention not described in specification.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents to be construed liberally, in fair sense of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are to be construed liberally and not with rigid or overly nicety; the nature and extent of the invention is to be ascertained by the fair sense of the words used by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts adopt a liberal and expanded view to promote the progress of science and useful arts; not to fritter rights away on purely technical objections. (Cited dicta from Justice Story and cases such as Ames v. Howard; Blanchard v. Sprague.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Two objects of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification has two objects: (1) to make known how to construct/use the invention so artisans can make and use it after patent expiry; (2) to put the public in possession of what the patentee claims so as to ascertain novelty and warn potential users of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These twin objects inform the rules of construction and the requirements of sufficiency and clarity in drafting. The specification must enable practice after expiration and disclose what is claimed to avoid misleading the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe subject-matter so public can know the claim (first rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification must describe the subject-matter — what the patentee claims to have invented — so as to enable the public to know what his claim is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language need not be technical or scientifically accurate but must not mislead and must show with reasonable certainty what is intended to be claimed. Whole specification must be read in connection; phrases standing alone should not be singled out. If the invention is left ambiguous and uncertain, the patent is void. (Wyeth v. Stone; Lowell v. Lewis.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description must distinguish old from new
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patentee uses what is old, the specification must distinguish between what is old and what is new and point out in what the invention consists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification mixes old and new without distinguishing and thereby appears to claim the whole as new, the patent may be broader than the invention and void. The patentee should, if using known elements, either omit them or designate them as old, or expressly disclaim them. (Dixon v. Moyer; Carpenter v. Smith; Davis v. Palmer.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Everything that appears to be covered by the claim is part of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever appears to be covered by the patentee's claim must be taken as part of the claim; courts cannot reject parts of a claim, and if anything claimed is not new the patent is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even small or unimportant asserted inventions, if included in the claim and found not new, will void the patent. (Cases cited: Moody v. Fisk.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrict claims to be co-extensive with actual discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification should be construed, consistently with the fair import of language, so as to make the claim co-extensive with the actual discovery; patentees will be presumed not to intend to claim things they know to be in common use unless language requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction should not extend claim beyond the true invention; the court should adopt interpretation that gives effect to the exact nature and extent of the claim as apparent in the whole instrument. (English Court of Common Pleas rule; Haworth v. Hardcastle.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Describing old matters: general reference allowed if not ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not always necessary to describe things that are old in detail; things generally known or in common use may be referred to in general terms provided they create no ambiguity and are accompanied by an intelligible description of what is new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing an improvement, the former machine should be set forth sufficiently to show what the patentee engrafts his improvement upon, and the patentee should disclaim the old and state distinctly the improvement claimed. Failing to do so risks making the patent appear to claim the whole machine. (Dixon v. Moyer; Godson on Patents.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vagueness in manner of describing invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A common defect is vagueness or ambiguity in the manner of description which makes it difficult or impossible to determine what the invention is (distinct from ambiguity in words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: directions that leave it uncertain whether several listed materials are to be treated together or separately (lead/minium/red lead); claiming a whole class of substances when in fact only one works will mislead the public and render the specification ambiguous. (Turner v. Winter; Ryan v. Goodwin.)

rubrics_metrics.name: If the specification professes to produce results it does not, patent is void
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent professes to make or produce particular substances or effects by the directed process and the process, as directed, does not produce what is professed, the patent is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: a specification claiming to make white lead by the same process as produces something else — if it does not in truth produce white lead, the patent is void. (Turner v. Winter; Ashurst, J.'s observation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic claims over materials: permissible if combination is new and patentee disclosed his own materials
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee states the substances he uses and there are still other substances that will produce the effect, a generic description that claims the class is not void for ambiguity or over-breadth provided the combination is new in respect to all substances referred to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The key is that the combination must be new and the specification must honestly present what the patentee used; courts will consider the intention as expressed on the face of the specification and the state of knowledge at the time. (Ryan v. Goodwin; Crossley v. Beverly.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not include unnecessary parts; excess can render specification void
rubrics_metrics.description: Inserting more parts than necessary (e.g., describing ten parts where four suffice) can make the specification void for including superfluous and confusing details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overly detailed or unnecessary inclusions may be taken against the patentee as attempting to monopolize more than invented or as misleading the public. (The King v. Arkwright; Bickford v. Skewes.)
